sentences.t: Banks: ICICI Bank's profit rose 22% to ₹16,333 crore and Axis Bank's rose 39% to ₹7,705 crore in Saturday's September-quarter results; HDFC Bank grew 5% and IDBI fell 39%.

Insurance: the agents' federation LIAFI has asked IRDAI to raise first-year commissions to as much as 35%, days after the regulator's draft proposed capping them at 20 to 25% and banning dark patterns on insurance websites.
Comments close 25 October.
Jio week: anchor investors bid Monday for India's largest-ever IPO (band ₹1,065 to ₹1,119, up to ₹30,213 crore).
Markets are shut Tuesday for Dussehra; the issue opens Wednesday and closes Friday; listing is set for 28 October.

Markets: SEBI moves the closing auction, running since August, to a 3:30-3:40 pm window from 7 December, and expiry-day derivative settlement goes back to the 30-minute average price used before August.

AI: DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash-1017, a 552-billion-parameter checkpoint it says beats its September model on all 11 of its reported benchmarks, and opened its web search and fetch APIs to all developers.
Vendor claims, labelled.

Macro: forex reserves fell $8.58 billion to $726.03 billion in the week to 9 October as the RBI defended the rupee at 94.95 per dollar; the central bank's October minutes on Wednesday explain its shift to a tightening stance.
Long read: Policybazaar began as a comparison shop against the agent's commission; it is now India's largest insurance seller, just as the regulator rewrites how insurance may be sold.
Read it.
Two weeks ago this market was falling on inflation fear; last week it rose 2.78% on an IT bounce, and the open question was whether profits would back the prices.

Saturday's bank results are the first real answer, and they mostly say yes: ICICI and Axis grew profit at four to eight times the pace HDFC Bank managed, and bad-loan ratios kept improving at the state-owned banks.

What the market may still be underpricing is the squeeze between two facts it holds separately: the RBI raised rates in October and turned hawkish, and this week's Jio issue pulls ₹30,213 crore of cash out of the same pool.
My confidence: moderate, because one Saturday of banks is not a season.
What would prove me wrong: an anchor book on Monday that struggles to fill, or management commentary this week flagging margin compression from the rate cycle.
Source: BusinessLine Q2 liveblog / Mint week ahead

ICICI Bank (India's second-largest private sector lender) reported a 22.28% rise in consolidated September-quarter profit to ₹16,333.18 crore (standalone up 20.1% to ₹14,843 crore), on strong loan growth, higher net interest income (the gap between what a bank earns on loans and pays on deposits) and better asset quality.
Axis Bank (India's third-largest private sector lender) did even better: consolidated profit up 39.4% to ₹7,704.67 crore (standalone up 37.6% to ₹7,003.28 crore).
HDFC Bank (India's largest private sector lender), the heavyweight, grew just 5% to ₹19,510 crore on a standalone basis, with net interest income up 10%.
Three side-plots matter.

YES Bank (the private lender rescued in 2020) posted a 65% profit rise to ₹1,080 crore, excluding the impact of a Supreme Court ruling on its ₹8,400 crore AT-1 bond write-off; AT-1 bonds (perpetual bank bonds that can be written off in a crisis) remain a live legal risk.
IDBI Bank (the lender majority-owned by LIC and the government) fell 39% to ₹2,205 crore as non-interest income moderated.

And state-run Central Bank of India (a large public sector bank) rose 21% to ₹1,469 crore, a day after the finance ministry said public sector banks made a record ₹1.98 lakh crore in FY26 with bad loans at a multi-decade low.
Why it matters to you: Banks are a third of the Nifty's weight, so their profit season sets the index's floor.
The spread between the fastest (Axis at 39%) and the slowest (HDFC at 5%) tells you the rally is rewarding loan growth and treasury gains, not size.
Watch Monday's reaction: results came after the weekend close.
Source: BusinessLine Q2 liveblog
SEBI's 15 October circular, read in full, reworks the closing auction session (a fixed window where orders pool and one closing price is struck) (CAS) that has run every trading day since August.
Today continuous trading stops at 3:15 pm and the ten-minute auction sets the close by 3:25 pm.
From 7 December, continuous trading runs to 3:30 pm and the auction moves to 3:30-3:40 pm: five minutes for all orders, then limit-only, with a random close between 3:38 and 3:40 pm to deter gaming.
The reference price stays the VWAP (volume-weighted average price, the average trade price weighted by size) of the last 15 minutes of continuous trading, as before.
Derivatives trading extends to 3:45 pm (expiring index contracts stop at 3:30 on expiry day; stock derivatives run to 3:45 daily), and a post-close session runs 3:50 to 4:00 pm at the closing price.
The bigger change is a U-turn on derivatives.
Since August, expiry-day settlement prices for index and stock contracts have been the auction's closing price; SEBI's September consultation then proposed blending that close with the old average.

After feedback, the regulator reverted: from 7 December, settlement prices are the volume-weighted average of the last 30 minutes of continuous trading, the method used for years before the auction existed, with exchanges publishing indicative values in real time.
New iceberg orders (large orders shown in small slices) stay banned inside the auction, and stop-loss orders are not allowed; unexecuted day orders carry in with priority.
The carried-order rules start 8 February 2027; everything else starts 7 December.
Why it matters to you: The closing price decides your NAV, your index fund's tracking and every derivative settlement.
The auction that sets it now sits at the very end of the session, and expiry-day settlements return to the average-price method the market used for years.
If you invest through mutual funds or ETFs, this quietly changes what 'the close' means.
Source: SEBI circular (primary) / Mid-day explainer

The timetable, from the RHP and exchange filings: anchor bidding Monday 19 October; the issue opens Wednesday 21 and closes Friday 23 October for everyone else, with a ₹2,500 crore quota reserved for Reliance Industries shareholders and ₹500 crore for employees; listing is scheduled for 28 October.
At the ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 band, Jio Platforms (the telecom and digital arm of Reliance Industries) is valued at roughly ₹10.3 trillion.
At up to ₹30,213 crore, the issue is India's largest, ahead of Hyundai Motor India's ₹27,857 crore issue in 2024.
The entire issue is fresh shares; up to ₹27,500 crore of proceeds repays borrowings.
Demand signals so far: Mint reported ADIA, QIA, GIC, Norges Bank, Mubadala, BlackRock and about 15 domestic asset managers seeking slots in the roughly ₹8,000 crore anchor book.
The grey market, an unofficial indicator, was pricing a premium of ₹221 a share on 16 October, implying a listing near ₹1,340, about 20% over the cap (investorgain.com, dated and unofficial).
The week is shortened: exchanges are shut Tuesday for Dussehra, with MCX running only an evening session from 5 pm (Goodreturns).
Why it matters to you: At ₹30,213 crore this is the largest public issue India has run, priced below street estimates to leave money for investors.
How the anchor book fills on Monday is the single best read on institutional appetite for Indian large-caps this quarter, and the issue pulls real cash out of the market in a holiday-shortened week.
Source: RIL filing (primary) / Mint week ahead / BusinessLine

The Life Insurance Agents' Federation of India (LIAFI) wrote to the IRDAI chairman on 15 October seeking first-year commissions of 27% for policies with premium terms of five to nine years, 30% for ten to fourteen years and 35% for fifteen years and above, plus renewal commissions of 7.5% in years two to six and 6% from year seven to maturity (Mint, citing an Economic Times report).

The letter argues the 'Insurance for All' goal needs a financially sustainable agency force, notes the average LIC agent earned about ₹16,774 a month in commissions, and says LIC's commission spend fell 4.55% in FY26 even as individual agents generated about 93% of its business.

The federation also opposed publishing agent-wise commissions on insurer websites, saying policyholders may then demand a cut of the commission, and asked for tighter oversight of corporate agents, banks and brokers, arguing mis-selling is not an individual-agent monopoly.
Its letter lands on top of the regulator's own draft, which proposes caps of 20 to 25% on first-year life commissions and a ban on website dark patterns.
Detail in the Insurance section.
Why it matters to you: This is the collision your desk lives on.
The regulator's distribution paper proposes commission ceilings and a dark-patterns ban; the largest agents' federation has answered with a formal demand for higher, legislated commissions.
What settles after the 25 October comment deadline will shape payouts, persistence and staffing across distribution.
Source: Mint on the LIAFI letter / LIAFI's own summary / Consumer Arena on the draft

DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash-1017 on 17 October, a post-training checkpoint of its V4.1-Flash model: 552 billion backbone parameters plus 196 billion 'Engram' parameters, activating 8 to 16 billion per token, with a one-million-token context window.

The company reports it beats the September checkpoint on all 11 benchmarks it published, scoring 77.0 on its DeepSWE coding test versus 74.0 for Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 in DeepSeek's own table; Claude still leads several reasoning benchmarks in the same table.
Alongside, DeepSeek opened its Search and Fetch APIs to every developer, giving agent builders a first-party web layer (MarkTechPost; benchmark figures are the vendor's).

NVIDIA, two days earlier, expanded its open Nemotron 3.5 family: Super VL, a 120-billion-parameter vision-language model for always-on agents, and two smaller Bolt models for local hardware, the 74B-A9B now and the 4-billion-parameter E4B on 23 October (NVIDIA blog, primary).
Why it matters to you: If you build or buy AI workflows, a credible cheap coding model plus a first-party web search layer behind one API key cuts the cost of agents that read the web.
Benchmark figures are DeepSeek's own and labelled as such.
Source: MarkTechPost (read in full) / NVIDIA blog (primary)
Beyond the headline numbers, three asks stand out.
One, renewal commissions running to policy maturity, framed as payment for long-term servicing, the exact duty the regulator says agents often abandon after the sale.

Two, a level field across channels: LIAFI alleges private insurers kept paying high commissions while some LIC policy payouts were cut to as low as 7% from October 2024, after maximum commission limits were removed in 2023.
Three, no public disclosure of individual agent commissions, which the federation says would invite policyholders to claim a share.
The timing is deliberate: IRDAI's distribution consultation closes 25 October, and chairman Ajay Seth has publicly promised an orderly transition with no intention to disrupt any market player.
The agent force is putting its number on the table before the final rules are drafted.

Why it matters to you: The demands quantify what the agency channel thinks survival costs: a 35% first-year ceiling on long-term policies is above what most private life insurers pay today, and the renewal ask (6% to maturity) is a pension for the agent force.
The letter also shows the channel's weakest flank: it resists commission disclosure to customers.
Source: Mint on the LIAFI letter / LIAFI's own summary

The IRDAI draft, summarised by Consumer Arena, would require insurers and large sellers to show product features, prices and quality information without first demanding a name, phone number or email, ending the industry-standard lead form that gates every quote.

It proposes banning dark patterns (interface designs that steer users into actions they did not intend) such as countdown timers and pre-ticked add-ons, with the regulator publishing what it finds, and it requires sellers to assess a buyer's needs and document why a recommended plan fits.

Proposed commission ceilings: for individual health insurance, up to 15% of first-year premium for distribution companies and 20% for agents (5% and 10% on renewal); for life insurance, 20% and 25% in the first year.
Everything here is a proposal open for comment until 25 October; final rules may differ.

Why it matters to you: If you sell insurance online, this redraws the funnel: features, prices and quality information must be visible before any personal details are collected, and manipulative design gets tracked and published.
Lead-generation economics change the day this becomes a rule.
Source: Consumer Arena on the draft / IRDAI

Indian startups raised $236.2 million across 25 deals between 12 and 16 October, up 92.2% from the previous week's $122.9 million (Inc42's tracker).
AI led with $53.4 million across six deals; ecommerce followed at $48.3 million.

The largest rounds: Boldfit, a D2C fitness brand, raised $41.8 million in a Series B led by Bharat Value Fund; GreenCell Mobility, an electric bus operator, raised $34.6 million from Impact Fund Denmark; RapidCanvas, an enterprise AI platform, raised $29 million in a Series B led by Vertex Ventures; Scimplify, a chemicals manufacturing platform, raised $25 million led by Hitachi Ventures; and Origin, a robotics startup, raised $20 million led by Accel, the week's most active investor with four deals.

Why it matters to you: The mix is the message: AI application-layer startups took the most money while the biggest single cheque went to a D2C fitness brand, so capital is funding both the AI buildout and proven consumer revenue.
If you are hiring or selling into startups, the money is in AI services and fitness.
Source: Inc42 weekly tracker
The draft's needs-matching clause creates a paperwork obligation for every sale: what the customer needed, what was offered, why it fit.

A voice-first copilot that sits in the agent's call, produces the assessment note, flags commission-conflicted recommendations and stores the audit trail is a compliance product the regulation itself creates demand for.
The wedge is the 25 lakh-strong agent force that LIAFI says cannot absorb more cost, which means the tool has to save time, not add it.
What would kill it: the clause diluted in the final rules, or insurers building it in-house first.
Why it matters to you: IRDAI's draft wants every recommendation to carry a documented needs assessment.
Whoever builds the tool that records, scores and archives that conversation sells into every insurer, broker and bank assurance desk in the country.
Source: Consumer Arena on the draft

In 1976, two finance professors at the University of Rochester, Michael Jensen and William Meckling, published a paper that explained half the conflicts in business with one idea.
'Theory of the Firm' asked what happens when one person, the principal (the one who delegates: the owner, the insurer, you), pays another person, the agent, to act on their behalf.
The agent knows more about his own effort than the principal ever can, and his interests are not the same.

The paper named the cost of that gap agency cost (the money lost when a hired hand's incentives diverge from the owner's): what the principal spends monitoring the agent, what the agent spends proving he is honest, and the 'residual loss' that remains anyway.
It became one of the most cited papers in economics and the foundation of modern corporate governance.
The mechanism shows up wherever effort is hard to watch.

Jensen and Meckling used it to explain why managers of listed companies build empires instead of paying dividends: they own little of the firm, so they keep little of the value they create but enjoy all of the perks they buy.

Their proposed fixes were the two levers that still run boardrooms: make the agent share the outcome (equity, commissions, bonuses) and make the outcome auditable (accounts, disclosure, independent directors).
Neither is free, and the paper's quiet warning is that the cheapest-looking contract usually just hides the residual loss.
This week's insurance news is the concept running in production.
A life insurer cannot watch what an agent says at a customer's kitchen table, so it pays commission: the agent shares the outcome.
But commission aligns the agent with the sale, not with the customer's need, which is how Yashish Dahiya's father ended up with policies that paid the agent and lapsed on the family.

IRDAI's draft attacks the same divergence from the other side: cap the commission, ban the dark pattern, and force a documented needs assessment, in other words more monitoring and less outcome-sharing.
LIAFI's letter defends the outcome-sharing lever, arguing a 35% first-year commission is what makes a village agent's economics work.
The regulator, the insurer and the agent federation are all arguing about the same dial Jensen and Meckling drew in 1976.

Applications beyond insurance: product managers designing sales incentives face it when the sales team optimises for the bonus metric instead of retention; investors face it in every fund whose manager charges fees on assets rather than outcomes; founders face it the day they hire a professional CEO.

The decision rule: when you cannot watch the work, pay on the outcome you actually want, audit the metric rather than the person, and assume any metric you pay on will be gamed, so keep it close to the real goal.
Sixty-second recall, closed book: (1) Name the three parts of agency cost.
(2) Why does paying commission not fully align an insurance agent with a customer?
(3) What two levers did Jensen and Meckling propose?
Answers: (1) monitoring, bonding, residual loss.
(2) Commission aligns him with the sale, not the suitability; his gain comes from the product sold, not the claim paid years later.
(3) Outcome-sharing pay and auditability.
Source: Jensen and Meckling 1976 (journal page) / paper PDF
Put Saturday's bank results through an AI second reader.
Download the HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank and Axis Bank results PDFs from the BSE announcements page, open a free NotebookLM notebook at notebooklm.google.com, and upload all three.

Ask it: 'Compare the three banks on net interest margin, credit costs and treasury income, and tell me which profit beat came from lending and which from one-offs.' Time: about 15 minutes including the downloads.

A good result is a one-paragraph answer you can defend: you should be able to say, in your own words, which of the three beats was driven by loan growth and which by treasury or provisioning swings, with the page number NotebookLM cites for each claim.
If the tool gives you a number without a source page, ask it for the citation before using the number.

It ends on the decision in front of its founders today.
